about: The three cases obstacle-avoiding grid routing gets wrong, laid out so each is a node's position rather than a graph property. Node positions are given explicitly, because a routing fixture is about GEOMETRY: which cells are obstacles, and whether a route can get past them. Read with grid_index::GridParams { resolution: 8, margin: 2, clearance: 0 }, under which the span 0..8 gives a cell of exactly 1 and a cell index is the coordinate. Node order is the order below, so a node's dense index is its position in `nodes`.

a_wall_across_the_middle.why: A route from west to east must go round. This is the ordinary case, and the one that would silently regress to a straight line through the wall if the obstacle rule were dropped.
a_wall_across_the_middle.wall: seven nodes at x = 7, y = 1 to 7, leaving gaps at y = 0 and y = 8

a_symmetric_wall.why: The same wall made symmetric about the line joining the endpoints, so the two ways round it cost EXACTLY the same. Equal-cost paths are the normal case on a uniform grid, not an edge case, and this is the fixture that forces the tie-break to be total: the route must be one specific answer, and the same one every run. Tests: routed::tests::a_symmetric_wall_makes_two_exactly_equal_detours_and_the_lower_cell_route_wins.
a_symmetric_wall.note: The wall in the end-to-end test is built in code rather than read from this file, because graph-core is pure and cannot read files; this records the geometry those tests construct.

an_enclosed_node.why: A node ringed by eight others, so every cell it could step into belongs to a node. No route exists, and the honest answer is the straight segment plus straight_fallback = true in the output struct — a downstream program reads that field, not a log line. The ring is at ONE cell spacing: at two, the ring is not sealed and the enclosed node walks out between the gaps, which is a different (and wrong) answer.
an_enclosed_node.ring: eight nodes one cell from the centre, at the four diagonals and the four axis neighbours

nodes.role: wall case: the gap at the bottom
wall case: directly ahead of the route
wall case: the gap at the top
enclosed case: the node with no way out

edges.case: wall: a route exists and must go round
wall: the two endpoints are adjacent, so the route is one step
enclosed: no route exists, straight_fallback is set
enclosed: adjacent, so a route does exist even from inside the ring
enclosed: a diagonal that must not pass through the hub
